newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: Malaysia gets set for electronic insurance trade.
newsitem.headline: Malaysia gets set for electronic insurance trade.

text.p: Malaysia will launch a fully integrated electronic trading system for the central administration and settlement of reinsurance premiums and claims payments by the end of the year, Deputy Finance Minister Wong Se Wah said on Wednesday.

Wong said the Central Administration Bureau (CAB) would handle all facultative reinsurances placed in the country in its first stage of implementation later this year, but could be extended to other sectors of the insurance business.

"Although CAB is being established for the electronic placement of reinsurance transactions in Malaysia, its information technology infrastructure could be used for wider information sharing and communication and managing risk exposures for a greaer spread of users," he said.
He told the second Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) Insurance Congress the system could also provide the foundation of an ASEAN-wide eletronic trading network for insurers.
"It should be worthwhile for CAB to explore the feasibility of providing other services, such as regional networking among insurers and reinsurers in ASEAN," he said.

Malaysia's insurance industry generated premiums of about US$1.8 billion in 1995, according to analysts and while a small proportion of this sum relates to reinsurance, the transaction volume could be significant.

Market watchers estimate the average number of transactions that need to be completed by each company involved in a reinsurance contract, including endorsements, premium and claims transactions, to be about 8,900 per year in Malaysia.
Insurers could save millions of dollars annually by centralising the transaction process.

CAB has been under development since October 1995 and the ambitious end of the year launch date would see Malaysia leapfrog ahead of its regional competitors to create a central processing bureau mirroring those in the London Market, the fous of the global insurance industry.
"This would bring Malaysia right up to speed with Lloyd's and the London Market," Roger Foord, principal consultant with London-based Rebus Group plc, told Reuters.
Foord, in Malaysia to launch Rebus's new RIS (Asia) unit and a former consultant to the CAB project, was upbeat about the new system's prospects.
"It's supported 100 percent by the local market, it's got the backing of Bank Negara and the Ministry. With that sort of backing it'll get off the ground," he said.
"The way it's designed means the system could easily be used for international business," he added.

Singapore, widely acknowledged to be the region's centre of reinsurance expertise and the base for more than 40 international market players, is planning its own bureau but market sources say a full-scale launch is still some way off.

The London International Insurance and Reinsurance Market Association (LIRMA) earlier this year began offering Asian branches of its 100 or so full ordinary members direct access to the bureau services provided by its London Processing Cntre (LPC) joint venture.
LPC handles premiums and claims in excess of US$10 billion a year for members of LIRMA and the Institute of London Underwriters (ILU) licensed in the European Union and European Economic Area.
